facts.claim: ACCC: consumer guarantees give consumer rights if a travel service is delayed or cancelled. They apply to travel services within Australia, travel services provided by international businesses that depart Australia, and travel services to Australia from another country booked through a travel provider's Australian website.

ACCC: these rights apply regardless of whether the consumer books directly with a primary travel service provider (such as an airline, cruise line or tour operator), through a travel agent, or through a third party or intermediary such as a booking platform or travel package provider.

ACCC: if a replacement travel service is not within a reasonable time, the travel service provider must give the consumer their choice of a different replacement service or a refund. There is no one set definition of 'a reasonable time'; the ACCC does not decide what is reasonable, which is the role of a court or tribunal.

ACCC: travel service providers do not have to give replacement services or refunds under the consumer guarantees if the consumer changes their mind or misses the service for reasons unrelated to it, or if the actions of a third party prevent the provider from supplying the service. In these situations the right to a refund or replacement generally depends on the booking's terms and conditions.

ACCC: if a consumer books through a travel agent or another intermediary, they should check the terms and conditions of the intermediary and of any primary travel service provider; both businesses' terms and conditions apply. Agents and intermediaries are usually bound by the primary provider's terms and, legally, may only need to pass on the remedy the primary provider offers.

ACCC tips when booking travel: check the terms and conditions of the travel service, and of your agent or intermediary if booking through one, before booking. Understand what you are entitled to if the provider delays or cancels, if you cancel or miss the service, and if the booking cannot proceed for reasons outside both parties' control ('force majeure'). If terms are unclear or cannot be found, contact the provider and ask them to confirm in writing; different terms may apply to different travel periods.
ACCC: if arriving on time is critical, consider a fare class with better options if there is a delay or cancellation, and allow extra time to reach the airport and between flight connections.

ACCC: the ACCC does not provide legal advice and does not resolve individual complaints about delayed or cancelled travel services. If a provider does not resolve a problem, the first step is to contact the provider to explain it, then take it further.

Smartraveller (page last updated 18/08/2026): the right travel insurance is as essential as a passport for travel overseas; get insurance regardless of who you are, where you are going and what you are doing. The Australian Government cannot pay your bills and expects all Australians travelling overseas to take out appropriate insurance.

Smartraveller: always read the Product Disclosure Statement (PDS) before buying a policy. It sets out what you are covered for (inclusions), what you are not covered for (exclusions), word definitions, how the claims process works and what emergency support is provided.

Smartraveller: choose a policy that covers every country you are travelling to, including stopovers and transit points, and check whether the policy covers cancellations if a destination's advice level goes up after you have booked.
Smartraveller: always declare everything upfront when you buy a policy, or you may void it; you must tell your insurer about all pre-existing health conditions.

Smartraveller: free credit card travel insurance often covers fewer situations with lower item limits than comprehensive policies; understand what it covers, how much and how to activate it, and do not assume it is activated.

Smartraveller travel insurance buying guide: if a circumstance, risk or event is known before you buy the policy, you will not be covered if it directly affects your travel. The earlier you buy travel insurance, the more likely you are to be covered if something unexpected happens at your destination before your trip.

Smartraveller travel insurance buying guide: travel agents and third-party booking sites have their own terms and conditions, which are the first port of call to determine eligibility for a refund or credit, but the fine print is still subject to Australian Consumer Law.

Smartraveller travel insurance buying guide: whether you can get money back from an airline, travel agent or booking site for changed or cancelled plans usually comes down to who makes the change. You are more likely (but not always) eligible for a refund or credit if the provider cancels; if you cancel or change plans it may be deemed 'change of mind'.

Smartraveller travel insurance buying guide: travel provider or agent insolvency is commonly excluded from cancellation cover, and only a few insurers cover the insolvency of a travel provider. Check with your travel agent whether they have insolvency insurance; it is not compulsory, so only some agents have it.

Smartraveller travel insurance buying guide: paying by credit card may help, as some banks allow a 'chargeback' (asking the bank to reverse a disputed transaction) if you do not receive what you paid for; do not accept contract terms that require you to give up chargeback rights.

Moneysmart (last updated 17 September 2026): when sending money overseas, providers choose the exchange rate they use and charge fees; costs depend on how much you send, where you send it and how you send it.

Moneysmart: compare the exchange rate (and whether the advertised rate is the rate you get), whether the rate is guaranteed, transfer fees and commission including any 'margin' to convert currency, whether the receiver pays fees, payment method and transfer time.

Moneysmart: in Australia, money transfer services must be registered with AUSTRAC; check a money transfer business is registered before using it. If a transfer goes wrong, contact the bank or business first, then complain to AFCA if they are a member. Money sent to a scammer is almost impossible to get back.

insider_details.detail: Read two sets of terms, not one. When a wedding trip or honeymoon is booked through an advisor, both the advisor's and each hotel's or airline's terms apply, so ask for the cancellation and change terms of every component in writing before you pay.

Buy travel insurance as soon as the trip is booked, not the week you fly. Cover depends on what was known when you bought the policy, and insolvency of a travel provider or agent is commonly excluded, so check the PDS for both.
For guests and the couple alike, the policy has to name every country on the route, stopovers and transit included; a European wedding with an Asian stopover needs both covered.
Pay deposits by credit card where the supplier allows it, and never sign terms that waive chargeback rights. Ask your advisor whether they carry insolvency insurance, because not all agents do.

Overseas supplier payments cost more than the exchange rate you see. Compare the rate actually applied, any margin and the fees on both ends before paying a venue balance offshore, and allow time for the transfer to land.
A single advisor who agrees the fee and confirms inclusions in writing, in your time zone and in AUD, is the practical way to get the written confirmations the ACCC recommends asking for.
